name: Csv::Parser
listed_description: Compile-time and runtime CSV parser written in C++17.
reason: No numeric comparison against any named baseline reachable. README (read in full) has no benchmark or timing; repo tree (catch2, csv_parser, doc, examples, tests) has no benchmark directory and doc/ holds only theme/ and CMakeLists.txt. Only performance remark is a README sentence that plugging in fast_float 'allows for improving the performance of parsing floating point numbers compared to the standard library', with no numbers. Searches for third-party CSV shootouts including it found none (results were about vincentlaucsb/csv-parser and other projects). 34 stars, Zlib licence.

name: curlcpp
listed_description: An object oriented C++ wrapper for CURL(libcurl).
reason: No numeric comparison against any named baseline reachable. README (read in full, grepped for fast, bench, perf, speed, slow, compar) is usage examples only. It is a thin object-oriented wrapper over libcurl, so the baseline it could beat is libcurl itself, and no wrapper-overhead or speed claim exists. A search for wrapper-overhead benchmarks versus raw libcurl found only a curl mailing-list remark that bindings should rarely cost significant speed, no numbers.

name: curlpp
reason: No numeric comparison against any named baseline reachable. Repo page (about 1.8k stars, MIT; cmake, doc, examples, extras, include, src; Readme.md) pitches exception safety, type safety and stdlib integration, with no performance claim or benchmark directory. It is a thin wrapper over libcurl, so it cannot be faster than libcurl. A pistack.xyz blog post of C++ HTTP client libraries that may mention it was EGRESS_BLOCKED, so its contents are unknown.

name: DuckX
listed_description: C++ library for creating and modifying Microsoft Word (.docx) files.
reason: No numeric comparison against any named baseline reachable. README (read in full, about 2 KB) says it was written because no C++ library parsed .docx properly; no speed claim, no benchmark. Search for DuckX versus python-docx, docx4j or LibreOffice speed found nothing; the numbers surfaced belonged to a different project (office_oxide vs python-docx).

name: FreeXL
listed_description: an open source library to extract valid data from within Spreadsheets.
reason: Home page www.gaia-gis.it is EGRESS_BLOCKED, so the official docs could not be opened. Package-index snippets describe a lightweight C reader for BIFF8 .xls with stated goals 'simple and lightweight, stable, robust and efficient', which is a directional claim with no numbers. Search for FreeXL versus libxls or other XLS readers found no published benchmark.

name: GNU Bison
listed_description: General-purpose parser generator that converts an annotated context-free grammar into a range of parsers.
reason: Bison is itself the incumbent yacc baseline. README (5 KB) has no performance claim. NEWS (165 KB, grepped for faster, speed, perform, benchmark, slower) has only self-comparisons against Bison's own defaults: api.token.raw saves one table lookup per token, 'in extreme cases (very simple user actions), a 10% improvement can be observed'; std::move in lalr1.cc gives 'a significant speedup' for large types, no number; glr2.cc is claimed 'upward compatible in terms of ... performance' to glr.cc. No named external baseline. Candidate third-party source: PLOS ONE 2022 'An empirical evaluation of Lex/Yacc and ANTLR parser generation tools' (Ortin et al.), but it is mainly a student-productivity study, and PMC, uniovi.es and the Lime comparison page were all EGRESS_BLOCKED, so no numbers could be read. Revisit if a network with PMC access is available.

name: hammer
reason: Only numeric comparison found shows hammer slower, not faster. README says only that the library supports 'Benchmarking for parsing backends' to pick the fastest backend for a grammar; no numbers and no comparison to yacc, bison or lex. Third-party suite rust-bakery/parser_benchmarks (Geal, nom author, mp4 directory, optimized build, late 2013 MacBook Pro 2.3 GHz quad-core i7, upstream UpstandingHackers/hammer) lists small.mp4: Hammer 32,424 ns/iter, Attoparsec 1,138, Cereal 184, Nom 240; bigbuckbunny.mp4: Hammer 26,523 ns/iter, Attoparsec 1,124, Cereal 181, Nom 195. The suite's README notes the hammer parser has slight memory leaks and parsers are written naively. Hammer is not in the HTTP or JSON directories. Retained here as not faster; a not-faster record could be written from that mp4 page if the orchestrator wants one.
